text: As of 20 August 2021, the user, who is from Arcadia, California, is considering pursuing a Master's degree in Computer Science and asked for information on the top CS programs in California.

The assistant listed seven top California CS programs: Stanford University; UC Berkeley (about an hour and a half drive from Arcadia); Caltech in Pasadena (about 20 minutes from Arcadia); USC in Los Angeles (about 30 minutes); UCLA (about 45 minutes); UC San Diego in La Jolla (about a 2-hour drive); and Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) Silicon Valley in Mountain View, which offers a Master's in CS focused on software engineering and data science.
The user attended Arcadia High School from 2010 to 2014, then attended UCLA for undergraduate study, so the user is familiar with the UCLA campus and its CS program.

The assistant said UC Berkeley's CS program has a strong research focus on theoretical computer science, AI, machine learning and data science, a large faculty, rigorous theory-heavy coursework with a strong emphasis on mathematical foundations, and a Bay Area location near Google, Apple and Facebook.

The assistant said UCLA's CS program has a more diverse research focus (AI, data science, computer networks, computer vision, human-computer interaction), a smaller faculty than Berkeley, a more balanced mix of theoretical and practical courses that are more applied and industry-focused, and a Los Angeles location with a growing tech industry.
The assistant estimated MS applicant acceptance rates of around 10-15% for UC Berkeley's CS program and around 20-25% for UCLA's, describing Berkeley's CS program as the more competitive of the two.

As of 20 August 2021, the user said they were leaning towards staying in SoCal, so UCLA was a strong contender, and asked about the projects and research opportunities available to CS students at UCLA.

The assistant listed UCLA CS research areas: AI and machine learning (deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision, robotics), data science and analytics, computer networks and distributed systems, computer vision and graphics, and human-computer interaction.

The assistant listed UCLA CS research opportunities: research assistantships for graduate students, research projects through courses, hackathons or independent studies, industry collaborations with companies such as Google, Facebook and Microsoft, the Startup UCLA Accelerator, and interdisciplinary work with Engineering, Medicine and Arts.

The assistant named UCLA research centers and institutes: the UCLA Artificial Intelligence Research Laboratory, the UCLA Center for Networked Systems, the UCLA Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics, and the UCLA Center for Health Policy Research.
As of 20 August 2021, the user said they were interested in AI and machine learning and asked about the faculty in UCLA's AI and ML research group and what they are currently working on.

The assistant named UCLA AI and ML faculty: Prof. Yizhou Sun (graph neural networks, recommender systems, anomaly detection), Prof. Song-Chun Zhu (visual perception, object recognition, human-computer interaction), and Prof. Cho-Jui Hsieh (scalable optimization, neural networks, robustness in machine learning).

The assistant named two more UCLA AI and ML faculty: Prof. Greg Ver Steeg (explainable AI, fairness in machine learning, causal inference) and Prof. Margo Seltzer (AI for social good, human-centered AI, AI ethics).
The assistant listed current UCLA AI and ML group projects: explainable AI, deep learning for computer vision, graph neural networks, fairness and bias in AI, and human-AI collaboration.

As of 20 August 2021, the user said they were particularly interested in explainable AI and fairness in AI systems, and asked whether they could get in touch with Prof. Ver Steeg or Prof. Seltzer about their research.

The assistant advised the user to contact Prof. Ver Steeg or Prof. Seltzer by email or through their personal websites, after reading their papers, introducing themselves, stating the goal of a UCLA Master's in CS, and showing enthusiasm, and provided an example email template.
As of 20 August 2021, the user said they would email Prof. Ver Steeg and Prof. Seltzer to request a meeting or call to discuss their research further.
The assistant advised the user to be themselves, be respectful and show enthusiasm, noting that professors appreciate proactive students who are genuinely interested in their research.

As of 20 August 2021, the user wanted to deepen their machine learning and AI skills, having already completed courses on Python programming, data structures and algorithms, and a Data Science specialization from Johns Hopkins University, and holding an Associate's degree in Computer Science from Pasadena City College (PCC) earned in May 2016 before joining UCLA.

The assistant recommended machine learning courses: Andrew Ng's Machine Learning course on Coursera, Machine Learning by Stanford University on Stanford Online, Andrew Ng's Deep Learning Specialization on Coursera, and Machine Learning with Python on DataCamp.

The assistant recommended AI courses: Artificial Intelligence (AI) by Columbia University on edX, AI for Everyone on Coursera, Natural Language Processing with Deep Learning on Stanford Online, Reinforcement Learning by Sutton & Barto on Udemy, and Deep Reinforcement Learning on Coursera.

The assistant recommended practice and reference resources: Kaggle competitions, TensorFlow and PyTorch tutorials, Machine Learning Mastery, the AI Alignment podcast, Towards Data Science on Medium, and the Machine Learning subreddit.

As of 20 August 2021, the user said they were interested in exploring computer vision. The assistant recommended computer vision courses: Computer Vision by University of Michigan (Coursera), Computer Vision by Stanford University (Stanford Online), Deep Learning for Computer Vision (Udemy) and Computer Vision with Python (DataCamp).

The assistant recommended computer vision books: Richard Szeliski's Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications, Adrian Rosebrock's Deep Learning for Computer Vision with Python, and David Forsyth and Jean Ponce's Computer Vision: A Modern Approach, plus CVPR, ICCV and IEEE TPAMI as leading venues.

The assistant recommended computer vision datasets and libraries: ImageNet, CIFAR-10, the Open Images Dataset, Kaggle Computer Vision Competitions, and the OpenCV, TensorFlow, PyTorch and Keras libraries.

As of 20 August 2021, the user said they were especially interested in object detection and segmentation. The assistant recommended courses: Object Detection and Tracking (University of Pennsylvania, Coursera), Object Detection and Segmentation (University of Michigan, Coursera), and Deep Learning for Object Detection (NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute), covering YOLO, SSD and Faster R-CNN.

The assistant recommended object detection tutorials (PyImageSearch on YOLO and SSD, and Matterport's Mask R-CNN tutorial), original papers on YOLO, SSD, Faster R-CNN and Mask R-CNN, and datasets PASCAL VOC (20 object classes), COCO (80 object classes) and the KITTI Object Detection Benchmark.

As of 20 August 2021, the user said they were interested in object detection using YOLO and asked for tutorials, papers and implementations. The assistant recommended YOLO tutorials: PyImageSearch's YOLO Tutorial, Machine Learning Mastery's YOLOv3 Tutorial using Python and Keras, and NVIDIA's real-time object detection tutorial using the Jetson TX2.

The assistant recommended YOLO papers (YOLO, YOLO9000: Better, Faster, Stronger, and YOLOv3: An Incremental Improvement) and implementations: the official YOLO repository (written in C), PyYOLO (Python with OpenCV), TensorFlow-YOLO and Keras-YOLO.
The assistant recommended YOLO videos and lectures: 3Blue1Brown's YOLO Explained, Sentdex's YOLO tutorial, and the Stanford CS231n lecture on object detection with YOLO.

As of 20 August 2021, the user said they wanted to explore YOLO for object detection in autonomous driving and asked for resources. The assistant recommended tutorials: NVIDIA's Object Detection for Autonomous Vehicles using YOLO, Machine Learning Mastery's YOLOv3 tutorial for autonomous vehicles, and Udacity's YOLO for Autonomous Driving, covering pedestrian, car and traffic light detection.

The assistant said NVIDIA's DriveWorks SDK for autonomous vehicles includes a YOLO-based object detection module, and recommended the KITTI, Cityscapes and Argoverse datasets for object detection in autonomous driving scenarios.

As of 20 August 2021, the user said they wanted to explore YOLO for pedestrian detection in autonomous vehicles and asked for resources. The assistant recommended tutorials: NVIDIA's Pedestrian Detection using YOLO, Machine Learning Mastery's YOLO-based pedestrian detection tutorial, and OpenCV's Pedestrian Detection using YOLOv3.

The assistant recommended pedestrian detection datasets (Caltech Pedestrian Dataset, Cityscapes Dataset, KITTI Pedestrian Dataset) and noted that NVIDIA's DriveWorks SDK includes a YOLO-based pedestrian detection module.
